The [IJCAI 2024 paper](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf) defines \(L=-[\log\sigma(s_+)^\beta+\sum_{j=1}^K\log(1-\sigma(s_j))]/(K+1)=[\beta\,\mathrm{softplus}(-s_+)+\sum_j\mathrm{softplus}(s_j)]/(K+1)\). Sampling rate \(\alpha=K/(|I|-1)\); calibration \(\beta=\alpha[t(1-1/\alpha)+1/\alpha]=1-t+t\alpha\). Thus \(t=0\) gives BCE; \(t=1\) gives \(\beta=\alpha\), theoretically calibrated under the sampling assumptions. The [official PyTorch implementation](https://github.com/asash/gSASRec-pytorch/blob/main/train_gsasrec.py) transforms positive logits with \(\gamma(s)=\log[1/(\sigma(s)^{-\beta}-1)]\), applies BCE, averages across all K+1 terms, then averages valid sequence positions. Its float64/clamping introduces numerical differences from the algebraic formula.

For K=64, the requested expression \(A=\beta\,\mathrm{softplus}(-s_+)+\mathrm{mean}_{64}\mathrm{softplus}(s_-)\) is **not** the paper loss. Paper loss is \(B=[\beta\,\mathrm{softplus}(-s_+)+64\,\mathrm{mean}_{64}\mathrm{softplus}(s_-)]/65\). Relative to negatives, A weights positives **64 times more heavily**; equivalently, A is proportional to paper gBCE with effective positive coefficient \(64\beta\). Multiplying the entire loss by 65 changes overall scale; replacing the negative sum with its mean changes the objective.

The [full paper’s theorem](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.07192) explicitly assumes uniform sampling **with replacement**, excluding the current positive; duplicates count, so alpha is expected multiplicity, not unique-item inclusion probability. Excluding each user’s entire training history changes support and invalidates the stated calibration guarantee. Moreover, the [official PyTorch sampler](https://github.com/asash/gSASRec-pytorch/blob/main/dataset_utils.py) samples all item IDs with replacement, allowing positive/history collisions. Derived consequence: its unconstrained optimum is \(\sigma(s_i)=\beta P(i)/(\beta P(i)+K/|I|)\), rather than the theorem’s \(\beta P(i)/[\beta P(i)+\alpha(1-P(i))]\); exact calibration therefore does not follow, although rare-item probabilities can approximate it.
